He added that the rumors also aim to embolden Iranians opposed to the regime, giving them “courage to come to the streets so that the plans of the U.S. and Israel can be realized.” Abdolreza Davari, a former adviser to the interior ministry and a vocal supporter of Mojtaba’s, told me that the leader is “in full health” and will soon be revealed to the public. But the two weeks with no communication, the public appeal for sheep sacrifice, and the rumors emanating from government circles have led many Iranians to doubt such assurances.

Whether Mojtaba is dead or alive, his public absence creates problems for the Iranian regime. The supreme leader holds most of the constitutional power in the Islamic Republic and has in the past served as the final arbiter among the system’s warring factions and institutions. Mojtaba appears to be sitting these conflicts out, at a moment when their outcome could be particularly consequential.

The country’s 13-person National Security Council is effectively running the country as a collective. It is chaired by Pezeshkian, a reformist who favors an end to the war with America, and includes Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the powerful parliamentary speaker who led the talks with the United States. But it also includes General Ahmad Vahidi, the head of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, and other military leaders.

Back in June, 12 of the council’s 13 members voted in favor of the memorandum of understanding that Iran reached with the United States in Islamabad. Mojtaba sent a message endorsing the deal but also noting that he had initially opposed such an agreement “in principle.” Hard-line critics of diplomacy seized on this to claim that Ghalibaf had usurped power and forced the memorandum on the leader. A news outlet linked to a faction in the IRGC even issued a documentary called Ghalibaf’s Coup.

Mojtaba neither endorsed this view nor put it to rest. Rather, he has remained mum as various factions have purported to speak for him. Pezeshkian has told reporters that in his meeting with Mojtaba, the leader stressed that regime officials should “keep unity and cohesion” and avoid infighting.

But the infighting goes on. In June, a statement signed by 63 of the 88 members of the Assembly of Experts, a clerical body tasked with supervising the supreme leader, admonished regime officials that none of them was authorized to act against Mojtaba’s “definite opinion.” At the same time, the statement called on any Muslim “who could gain access” to kill Donald Trump—not quite the message of Iran’s negotiators, but rather more consonant with Mojtaba’s statements promising “blood revenge.”

The Iranian regime has existential choices to make as it decides between diplomacy and conflict. Iran’s constitution is clear about who has the authority to set the country’s course. But no one seems able to say for sure whether that person is alive or dead. And without a firm hand at the top, indecision can become a purgatory without a foreseeable end.

entries.title: The Jews Who Voted for Hitler
entries.summary: What happened when members of a minority community cast its lot with a political leader who despised them
entries.content:
What happened when members of a minority community cast its lot with a political leader who despised them

On the evening of February 5, 1930, the art and theater critic Paul Fechter took the podium before the League of Nationalist German Jews, in Berlin, to discuss purported Jewish control of the press and the arts in the country. “When Dr. Max Naumann invited me to give a lecture in your circle, I rather impulsively said yes,” Fechter began. “When he then told me the topic he wanted me to address, my immediate reaction was: Good grief ! One could not have found a better topic for making oneself thoroughly unpopular and for antagonizing everyone in the room.”

For too long, Fechter said, people had been too “shy, fearful, cautious” to speak openly about the Jews. Fechter, an editor at the conservative newspaper Deutsche Allgemeine Zeitung, was pulling no punches. The popular Jewish humorist Kurt Tucholsky, Fechter said, had insulted the German people with his recent book, Deutschland, Deutschland über alles, an acid satire about the army, the police, the civil service, the national anthem, even Sekt, a popular sparkling wine.

“A large portion of the literary and art worlds are in Jewish hands,” Fechter continued. “The theaters, the major publishing houses, the major art dealers are all at least partially under Jewish control.” Jewish art dealers, Fechter said, filled their galleries with works by “Manet and Monet and Renoir and Gauguin and Picasso and Cezanne”—French Impressionists and Modernists, in other words, rather than traditional German painters. The Antigermanismus among Jews, Fechter declared, was “far more robust” than the Antisemitismus among right-wing German nationalists.

Naumann, the founder of the league, published the Fechter tirade in his monthly publication, The Nationalist German Jew, circulated to his group’s 7,000 members, mostly middle-class professionals in more than 20 chapters around the country. Naumann himself was a Berlin-based Jewish attorney who was decidedly antidemocratic, belligerently nationalistic, and unapologetically critical of other Jews.

He blamed Ostjuden—the “Eastern Jews” fleeing pogroms in Russia, Romania, Austria, Hungary, Poland, and elsewhere—for flooding the country with unwanted immigrants. He felt pity but no solidarity. “It is the same pity we feel when there is talk of the Turks massacring Armenians or of lynch mobs targeting black people in America,” Naumann wrote—an abstract pity without emotional connection. In his league’s founding treatise, On Nationalist German Jews, published in 1920, Naumann had compared Zionists, those seeking a Jewish homeland in Palestine, to Nazis, whose political movement had just been founded. “Both groups, the fanatics of Zion and the knights of the swastika, are basically the same in that they have turned a question of ancestry into a question of nationality,” Naumann argued.

Naumann defended his German and Jewish identities in equal measure, a stance reflected in the term nationaldeutscher Jude—a blood-and-soil German Jew.

Naumann drifted right with the rest of German politics in the early 1930s, first abiding and then supporting the extremist, right-wing, rabidly anti-Semitic positions of Adolf Hitler. It is impossible to imagine a more tragically misplaced political calculation than Naumann’s embrace of national socialism. Though the Hitler Juden—or Nazi Jews, as Naumann’s adherents came to be known—represented less than 2 percent of Germany’s half-million Jews, they provide a cautionary tale of members of a minority within a minority who cast their lot with a political leader who openly despised them.

Naumann was born in 1875 into a middle-class family—bankers, landowners, cloth merchants—in an era of unprecedented opportunity for German Jews. They had recently gained the right to vote. They could run for office. They enjoyed equal protection under the law. Professions formerly restricted were now open—law, medicine, academia. Naumann studied jurisprudence at the Friedrich Wilhelm University of Berlin, where he joined a fraternity and was given a Schmiss across his chin, the honorific dueling scar of a true Prussian. But prejudice persisted.

When Naumann was denied an officer’s title in the Prussian military because of his Jewish heritage, he enlisted in the 2nd Bavarian Infantry Regiment. Naumann advanced through the ranks, from lieutenant to first lieutenant and eventually to captain, serving with distinction during the First World War. He was awarded an Iron Cross First Class and an Iron Cross Second Class, among other decorations, for “outstandingly brave deeds performed in the face of the enemy that went far beyond the call of duty.”

But Jewish veterans of the Great War returned to find Jews collectively vilified for Germany’s defeat and surrender. The Reich Federation of Jewish Front-Line Soldiers countered with an information campaign highlighting their commitment and sacrifice—100,000 Jewish soldiers had served at the front; 35,000 had been decorated for bravery; 12,000 had given their lives for the fatherland. The Central Association of German Citizens of Jewish Faith, or Centralverein, sought to combat rising anti-Semitism through legal protections of Jewish identity and heritage. Meanwhile, the Zionist Federation of Germany urged German Jews to immigrate to Palestine for their own safety.

Naumann found these responses wholly inadequate or misguided. He denounced the members of the Centralverein as ineffective “Dummköpfe,” or idiots, and the Zionists as traitors, foremost among them “the world-famous scholar Einstein,” who placed his Jewish identity over his German heritage. “The spiritual and even the material misery of the Jews in Germany would never have assumed such frightening proportions,” Naumann claimed in 1927, “if steps had been taken in time to prevent the Zionists, and especially the Zionist Ostjuden, from positioning themselves before Jews and non-Jews alike as the only rightful spokesmen of Judaism.”

Naumann believed that anti-Semitism needed to be “dismantled,” not legally challenged, the Centralverein’s preferred approach. During the war, Naumann had watched anti-Semitic sentiment evaporate in the heat of battle, where what mattered, he later recalled, were “actions,” not “words,” and where “a tough, resilient, determined willingness to put one’s head on the line” for comrades and the fatherland “transcended all class and racial difference.” This was the experience that shaped his approach to German politics.

He was joined by Alfred Peyser, the chair of the League of Nationalist German Jews, who was also an eminent physician and the municipal counselor of an upscale Berlin district. In a foundational 1922 essay defining the concept of a “nationalist German” Jew, Peyser warned fellow Jewish Germans against returning to “Ghettoknechtschaft”—enslavement to the ghetto—or trying to escape to “Zion,” urging them instead to embrace the “German fatherland.” “Yes, we love this land, its language, its people,” Peyser wrote. “We feel as one with it!”

Naumann and Peyser found a powerful ally in Samuel Breslauer, the editor of the Berliner Lokal-Anzeiger, a popular conservative newspaper. Breslauer traveled to New York City in the spring of 1927 with a delegation of German newspaper editors to meet with their American counterparts, including Adolph Ochs, the publisher of The New York Times. Breslauer advocated for fierce German nationalism and equally fervent Judaism. He defended this duality in an article titled “Me, an Antisemite.” “If over the course of three decades I have undergone a change,” Breslauer wrote, it had been a political drift to the right—but “certainly not” away from Judaism. Instead, he insisted, his Judaism had deepened and strengthened—“in the religious, not in the ethnic-national sense.”

Naumann had initially aligned his league with the German People’s Party, a center-right party led by the Nobel laureate Gustav Stresemann. But the political picture changed in September 1930, when the National Socialists surged nearly tenfold in national elections. Fascism was suddenly fashionable. Siegfried “Fred” Bon, the Jewish author of a three-volume philosophical treatise, Does 2 x 2 = 4?, sought to square Judaism and national socialism. In a January 1931 article for The Nationalist German Jew, Bon cataloged Jewish contributors to the country’s conservative movements, foremost among them Walther Rathenau, a foreign minister in the Weimar Republic and the first person, according to Bon, who’d sought to merge nationalism with socialism—“the very positions that today constitute the foundations of the National Socialist program.” Bon’s article appeared under the title “Can Jews Be National Socialists?”

Naumann, for his part, suggested that they could be, and he pointed to Italy as evidence. Jews had joined Benito Mussolini in the 1922 March on Rome. Guido Jung, a Jew, was Italy’s fascist minister of finance. Renzo Ravenna, a Jew, was the fascist mayor of Ferrara. When Girolamo Bassi, a Jewish lawyer in Venice, faced financial difficulties, a judge suggested that he join Mussolini’s Partito Nazionale Fascista. “So, two months later, my father became a cardcarrying Fascist,” Bassi’s son Roberto later recalled, “and having bought a fine black uniform went with the others to demonstrate support for Il Duce.”

Naumann attributed the fascist receptiveness toward Jews in Italy not only to the absence of Zionists and Ostjuden in that country but also to Jews’ absence from “intellectual” professions. Naumann urged young German Jews to pursue careers in trades such as carpentry and masonry rather than professions such as law and medicine. “Of the approximately 200,000 Jews in Italy, at most 10% are doctors, lawyers, and journalists,” The Nationalist German Jew reported in a 1933 article titled “Why There Is No Hatred of the Jews in Italy.” (Although it’s true that there was less anti-Semitism in Italy than in Germany, the article’s premise would be proved grimly wrong when Italy passed a series of discriminatory racial laws starting in 1938 and deported Jews to Nazi extermination camps.)

In July 1932, Naumann caused a sensation when he appeared to urge German Jews to vote National Socialist in the upcoming Reichstag elections. In an article in Fechter’s newspaper, Naumann claimed that national socialism was the only viable future for the country—“that here, and only here, a path is being forged that can lead to a rebirth of Germanness and to the restoration of German prestige.”

Centralverein was outraged. An op-ed in the organization’s newspaper, Central-Verein-Zeitung, lambasted Naumann for inaccuracy and irresponsibility, and argued that to discount the threat posed by Nazi anti-Semitism was absurdly credulous. Whatever common values Naumann shared with Hitler—anti-communist, antirepublican, antidemocratic—hatred of Jews remained foundational to Nazi ideology. Central-Verein-Zeitung reminded Naumann of the Nazis’ “unbridled attacks” and “public incitement” against Jews, noting that “Herr Hitler has never, on any occasion, contradicted the speakers of his own party regarding their stance on the Jewish question.”

But Naumann continued to believe that the heated rhetoric against the Jews was political posturing that would cool once Hitler was in office, and once the inciting political effects of Jewish Communists, socialists, and Zionists had been neutralized. A trove of about 11 million digitized National Socialist records, analyzed by an international group of scholars from Harvard and elsewhere in a National Bureau of Economic Research paper published last April, includes 580 personal statements by Nazis, given in 1934, explaining their reasons for joining the party. Fully 26 percent of these Nazis cited their dislike of Jews as an “explicit causal reason” for joining the party, which suggests that anti-Semitism was considerably more than an incidental element of the party’s ideology. But Naumann was fixated on the other motivations for joining the party, which are reflected in the scholars’ analysis of these statements: 63 percent cited a hope for national renewal and the restoration of public order, while 53 percent expressed a desire for social belonging, 49 percent the need to combat communism, and 29 percent the belief that the party could lift them out of economic hardship. Naumann’s fatally naive view was that if these other concerns could be addressed, anti-Semitism would be diminished.

Following Hitler’s appointment as chancellor, in January 1933, anti-Semitic violence spiked horrifically. Jews were assaulted on the street, at their places of business, in their homes. One young man was lashed bloody, then had pepper rubbed in his wounds to heighten the agony; he died of sepsis. An apartment on Berlin’s fashionable Friedrichstrasse was repurposed as a torture room, its walls spattered with blood.

The foreign press chronicled the atrocities prominently. On March 25, Hermann Göring, the powerful Nazi cabinet minister, summoned Naumann and other Jewish leaders to his office. Göring read from a stack of foreign-newspaper clippings with growing fury. “Unless you put a stop to these libelous accusations immediately,” Göring said, “I shall no longer be able to vouch for the safety of the German Jews!” Naumann had intended to use the meeting to protest the rising anti-Semitic violence; to that end, he confronted Göring with a list of attacks on Jews. But he left the meeting as a propagandist for the Third Reich. “While we readily acknowledge that there are excesses against German Jews,” Naumann declared in a public statement, “we are not interested in foreign interference in our internal affairs.”

To his fellow Jews of German heritage, Naumann counseled patience. “Today we are enduring without question days of rage,” he wrote in May. “It was inevitable that this anger—built up and heightened over fourteen years—would initially erupt in an explosive outburst.” But Naumann anticipated the day, “in the not too distant future,” when the country’s anti-Semitic fever would break and “Aryan and Jew” would once again “join hands” in common cause for the fatherland. “When this day of self-reflection finally arrives,” Naumann wrote, “that will be the beginning of the real answer to the German Jewish question.”

The preceding month, however, Hitler’s government had enacted the Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service, which banned “non-Aryans” from government posts, as well as the Law on Admission to the Legal Profession, which prevented Jews—including Naumann—from practicing law. The Law Against Overcrowding in German Schools and Universities, passed at the same time, restricted the enrollment of Jewish students.

Amid these draconian measures, Hans Heinrich Peyser, the son of Alfred Peyser, ran into Naumann one day on the Berlin subway. Naumann was just returning from a meeting with leaders of the Nazi storm troopers. He spoke to Peyser of the Nazis’ “high ideals” and the need to try to understand things from their perspective. “I found this excessive self-absorption and inward-looking preoccupation, in light of what had already happened in Germany, to be absolutely grotesque,” Peyser wrote.

The Jewish Telegraphic Agency, in New York, a wire service covering the global Jewish community, viewed Naumann and his adherents with similar dismay. “Although their professions have been taken away from them, and although they live in a state of rigid suspense and fear of the moment when they will be humiliated, beaten, or imprisoned, a large number of German Jews continue to remain faithful to the fatherland,” the agency reported on August 13. The report noted Naumann’s denunciation of Zionists as “traitors to their country.”

Stories circulated of “Naumann Jews” ending their meetings with Hitler salutes and the singing of “Horst Wessel Lied ,” the Nazi Party anthem. Though Naumann dismissed the alleged singing as “Jewish horror stories,” he defended the stiff-armed salutes and the presence of Nazi banners, saying that Jews needed to “overcome their fear of the swastika”: “After all, the Christian cross,” he wrote in April 1934, is also a symbol “in opposition to Judaism,” but “for a long time now no reasonable Jew has refused to accept the Iron Cross or other cross-shaped decoration.”

In August of that year, when Reich President Paul von Hindenburg died, Naumann urged Jews to approve a public referendum transferring Hindenburg’s powers to Hitler in his capacity as chancellor, effectively handing Hitler unchallenged dictatorial rule. (He did so despite acknowledging to his fellow Jews that the Nazi regime had “brought rigors to us.”) “We urge all Jews who feel themselves Germans to vote ‘Yes’ on Aug. 19,” Naumann declared.

Naumann reaffirmed his solidarity with Hitler’s government the following week, when he dispatched a telegram to the Nazi leader informing him that the League of Nationalist German Jews would not be attending a conference in Geneva for the establishment of the World Jewish Congress. Learning of this, Pariser Tageblatt, a newspaper for anti-Nazis in exile, responded: “Thank God!”

A Gestapo report on a meeting of 400 nationalist German Jews in Berlin on May 27, 1935, confirms that Naumann’s support for Hitler persisted. Naumann “emphasized in particular that the members considered themselves genuine Germans,” the report noted, and “had welcomed the transformation in Germany brought about by the Führer.” The meeting ended with a rousing chorus of “Deutschland, Deutschland über alles.”

For all Naumann’s efforts to win approval or recognition from Nazi leaders for his organization, or for his view on what Jews’ place in the Third Reich should be, he never received any.

On September 15, 1935, Hitler’s government introduced the Reich Citizenship Law and the Law for the Protection of German Blood and German Honor, collectively known as the Nuremberg Laws, stripping Naumann and half a million other Jewish Germans of their citizenship. By then, Naumann was divorced, and his daughter had broken irreparably with him over his pro-Nazi position.

On November 18, Naumann’s league was forcibly disbanded. Naumann himself was arrested by the Gestapo that same day and taken to Columbia-Haus, an SS detention and torture facility. A few weeks later, after attempting to commit suicide by slitting his wrists with the glass from his spectacles, Naumann was released. He died of cancer in May 1939, isolated and abandoned.

By that point, thousands of Jews had escaped abroad. Alfred Peyser was stripped of his medical license and briefly incarcerated before immigrating to Sweden in 1939, where he survived the war. Other Naumann Jews were not so fortunate. Siegfried “Fred” Bon was dispatched to the Theresienstadt concentration camp in September 1940; he was executed there in April 1944. Samuel Breslauer, who lost his editorial post and his property to the Nazis, also perished in Theresienstadt, along with his wife, Bertha.

Naumann’s remains were interred in a Protestant cemetery in the town of Stahnsdorf, southwest of Berlin, where his headstone still stands. It bears his name and military rank, along with his dates of birth and death, but no indication of faith or family. Persecuted and forgotten as a Jew, he was buried as he’d wished to be—as a German.

This article appears in the October 2026 print edition with the headline “The Jews Who Voted for Hitler.”

entries.title: Darline Graham Is Not Her Brother
entries.summary: Thrown into office and an unexpected campaign, she is running on her brother’s legacy—but making clear that she’s different.
entries.content:
Thrown into office and an unexpected campaign, she is running on her brother’s legacy—but making clear that she’s different.

It’s something that happens so often in politics that there’s a name for it: widow’s succession. Dozens of times over the past century, women have filled a seat previously occupied by their late husband, and some have gone on to serve a long career.

What has never happened in Congress before is what Darline Graham is doing: a sister’s succession.

Less than 48 hours after Senator Lindsey Graham died suddenly from heart issues last month, South Carolina Governor Henry McMaster appointed Graham’s younger sister to complete the remaining six months of his term. Soon after that, Darline Graham announced that she would also run for a full six-year term, a bid that came at President Trump’s request. In the solidly red state, her biggest hurdle is likely to come in a primary runoff today. She is running in part on the legacy of her brother—but also in ways that bear no resemblance to the way he approached the job. Where he was chatty and seemed to love campaigning, she is reserved and describes the campaign as “brutal.” Where he was the ultimate Washington insider who served in Congress for more than 31 years, she is running as a populist outsider who previously worked with the disabled and visually impaired. And where he was one of his party’s most prominent and outspoken foreign-policy hawks until the day he died, she has conceded to having no experience and not much interest in such matters.

“I’m not that informed on national security,” she said during a debate last week, a blunder that has become a focal point in the final days of an abbreviated campaign. The president came to her defense, praising her for being honest. He has invested significant time and political capital in attempting to give her a late boost in a closer-than-expected primary race.

Her late brother comes up during almost every public event she holds—“I knew I could not sit on the sidelines. That’s not how Lindsey and I were raised,” she’s said—and campaign mailers tout that she is “Prepared to Carry on Lindsey’s Legacy.” She tells voters that “no one can ever fill his shoes” but that she will earn his seat. “I don’t just expect it to be handed to me,” she said earlier this month after casting her ballot in the special primary election.

Her Republican primary opponent is Ralph Norman, a congressman since 2017 who earlier this summer lost his bid for governor. He has also referenced Lindsey Graham’s pull on the race. “Nobody’s entitled by birthright to this office,” Norman said before the debate last week. “You’ve got to earn it.” He tried to put the situation into college-football terms during an interview with the Associated Press, telling voters to imagine presenting the head coach at Clemson University with a top quarterback prospect who has just this qualification: They’re kin to Tom Brady. “Tell me how that analogy doesn’t work here,” Norman said. Although Graham has a famous last name and the president’s endorsement, Norman and his supporters believe that he can win today. Their message: Darline Graham is not Lindsey Graham. A PAC supporting Norman recently began running an ad that asks, “What if Darline Graham had any other last name?”

It’s the last name that has gotten her here—the reason she was appointed interim senator. But in the final stretch of the race, it is complicating her campaign, which has become the latest test of the power of Trump’s endorsement. Although the president has often played kingmaker in Republican primaries over the past decade, that influence has significantly weakened: 10 of his picks have failed to advance this year, many of them in the past few weeks. The congressional candidates Cory Mills and Catalina Lauf both lost in Florida last week. Two of his picks in races for governor—Megan Degenfelder in Wyoming and Mike Lindell in Minnesota—lost by double digits. If Graham loses, it will signal a limit to Trump’s ability to direct the MAGA base in one of the most MAGA states.

The relationship between Lindsey and Darline was long ago condensed into a few stock lines in their stump speeches: how they grew up in a one-room home that was attached to the bar and restaurant their parents ran. How their parents both died when Lindsey was in college, and how he took responsibility for helping raise his sister, who was nine years his junior. “Lindsey has been there for me throughout the years,” she said at the Iowa State Fair during his long-shot 2016 presidential campaign. “He has never let me down since then. He’s always been by my side.” Her remarks were earnest. And then he jumped to the stage with a joke: “Well, as Darline said, we grew up in a pool hall, a bar, and a liquor store. I’m eminently qualified to be president of the United States!”

A more textured version of their relationship emerges in a memoir he released during that campaign. He tells of how he arranged for her to have golf lessons, so that she could play one of his favorite sports. He took her to the movies (they both loved James Bond). He taught her to ride a bicycle when she was 5—then gifted her a turquoise one when she turned 9. In the early 1970s, he wrote, he heard his young sister use a racial slur. “She didn’t even think the term was offensive. She had heard it used so often,” he wrote. “I told her to not say it again, and a little while later, I went to my parents and asked them to make a change.” Graham says his mother offered a beer to a Black customer, who previously would have taken his beer home, and motioned to him to take a stool, slowly beginning to more actively integrate the barroom.

Graham also wrote of persuading his parents to take Darline to Disney World, a trip that became their first big family vacation. (Years later, in March 2026, the senator went viral for riding Space Mountain and carrying a bubble wand around during a government shutdown.) It was his and Darline’s first time on an airplane, and they stayed for five days at a Howard Johnson’s hotel with a pool. “Life was good. Then it wasn’t,” he wrote. The next year, his mother died. Shortly after, so did his father; it was Darline who found his unresponsive body, Graham wrote.

Lindsey Graham would go on to a career in the Air Force and then in Congress. His sister would earn a master’s degree in rehabilitation counseling from South Carolina State University, in Orangeburg, a historically Black school. She got her optician’s certification and in recent years led the South Carolina Commission for the Blind, which provides vocational, youth, and prevention services. She married her husband, Larry Nordone, in 2006, and they have two daughters. Darline kept her maiden name, she said recently on the campaign trail, as a way to feel connected to her parents.

The closest parallel that I could find to what Darline Graham is doing is this: When Representative Sonny Bono died during a family ski trip in 1998, his widow, Mary Bono, ran for his seat with the backing of Republican leaders. “It was crazy. It was a lot,” she told me. She got cotton mouth during her first debate but was so nervous that her shaky hand couldn’t bring the glass of water to her lips. “You’re told, It’d be great to be elected and fulfill the legacy of the loved one that was lost. But it’s really obvious on the campaign trail that only goes so far,” she said. “You have to establish who you are, what you care about, and show voters your own philosophies.” She won the race—and then, on the Judiciary Committee, she sat next to Lindsey Graham. “He had such a great and quick wit,” she said. Of Darline Graham, Bono told me: “I’m glad she’s running. But it will have to become her legacy and her work. It’s a hard job.”

Darline Graham has talked about the difficulty of campaigning while grieving, saying that she has not had time to fully process her brother’s death. She has said that sometimes, in the morning, she has time to reflect: “I think a lot about what I would say to him.” She remarked to a crowd at a barbecue joint in Florence, South Carolina, that she’d lost 10 pounds during the monthlong campaign following her brother’s death. “It’s been absolutely brutal. This past month has been brutal,” she said during a speech after making it to the runoff, one month after her brother’s death. “None of this has been comfortable for me. But like I said, I’m a fighter.” Her campaign and Senate office did not respond to my inquiries.

In South Carolina, an open Senate seat is rarer than a restaurant that doesn’t serve sweet tea. Strom Thurmond and Fritz Hollings had a combined tenure of more than 85 years, spanning most of the second half of the 20th century. Graham has occupied the seat since 2003. Longtime political operatives see Darline as quite different from her brother, although voters may be willing to overlook that if she can put forward a convincing case of her own. “Lindsey was the unique character in the public spotlight for decades. He was convivial. He was kind of a backslapper, wisecrack. Could deflect. Self-effacing,” Chip Felkel, a veteran Republican strategist in the state, told me. “I don’t see her personality that way, but I don’t think people care if she delivers for the state.”

The way Darline Graham is running her campaign reflects the ways she is trying to both align herself with her brother and differentiate herself from him. Her stump speech includes nods to the Second Amendment (“I believe gun control is how steady you hold your weapon”), a nod to voter-ID laws (“If you have to have an ID to check out a library book, you should have to have one to vote”), and transgender policies from her experience as a self-described volleyball mom (“I love watching my daughter play, and I know that boys have no place in girls sports, especially not in the locker room”). She has said that her No. 1 priority is “affordability” (a word that Trump has described as a hoax made up by Democrats). She wants to control health-care costs. She has also pointed to differences with her brother, saying that she would favor getting rid of the filibuster, something that he resisted, and that she would take a tougher line on immigration. Her brother supported creating a clearer pathway to citizenship. “I love Lindsey to death, but I’m a little bit stronger on immigration,” she said during a campaign event last week. “To me, it’s really clear; it’s a black-and-white issue: It’s legal versus illegal. If you’re here illegally, you should be deported. You’re breaking the law.”

As Trump prepared to fly to Myrtle Beach on Friday night for a Graham rally, he suggested to reporters that although “she’s a terrific woman,” it’s difficult for voters to get excited about her. The president’s message to voters at the rally: “What I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot.” Once he arrived in South Carolina that night, the memory of Lindsey Graham hovered. The late senator was the reason Trump knew Darline and that so many in the state knew her, the president said. Twice, he announced: “I’m doing this to honor Lindsey.” He asked voters to do the same.

“For Lindsey,” he said, “I want it to happen.”

Jack Rodriquez-Vars contributed research to this report.

entries.title: Trump Is Losing Touch With the Public
entries.summary: As the president spends less time with his base at rallies, his populist instincts are failing him.
entries.content:
As the president spends less time with his base at rallies, his populist instincts are failing him.

This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.

One of the few issues that unites voters and politicians of both parties right now is data centers. Three-quarters of Americans would oppose a data center being built near where they live, according to a new poll released last week by Heatmap Pro and Embold Research. The two leading lights of the left, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Senator Bernie Sanders, have sponsored a bill in Congress to create a temporary moratorium on new centers. They have an unlikely ally in archconservative Governor Greg Abbott of Texas, who said yesterday on ABC’s This Week that data-center companies “basically dug their own grave” and “got the backlash they deserve.”

Standing against this consensus is Donald Trump. The president remains a big booster of data centers. “Communities that don’t take a data center—they’re making a mistake,” he said Thursday during an interview with his on-again, off-again lackey Michael Cohen. “Data centers throw off tremendous amounts of jobs and money.”

This was no one-off. Trump had made several similar comments recently. “If I were the mayor of a town or the governor of a state and I had a chance to get a big plant in, an AI plant or a data center, I would absolutely want it, because the jobs are enormous and the money paid, the taxes paid, are just enormous,” Trump said last week—although he allowed that the sector could use “a little public-relations help.”

This puts Trump, the most successful demagogue in American political history, in the unusual position of misreading, and opposing, a populist groundswell. During his 2016 presidential campaign, Trump took many stands that were unpopular among establishment politicians. Some of these positions put him at odds not only with Democrats but also with most Republican elected officials. Trump broke with Republicans in claiming that he would protect social-welfare programs such as Medicare and Social Security, and he broke a bipartisan consensus by attacking free-trade agreements and promising protectionism. On these matters (as well as on his willingness to encourage and participate in gutter racism), Trump demonstrated that a big constituency existed for views that other politicians had deemed electoral liabilities.

Data centers’ political arc has been different. Initially, many officials seemed to back the centers, following exactly Trump’s logic: They offered jobs and tax benefits. But as public opinion turned—driven by a mix of backlash to AI in general, environmental concerns, worries about energy prices, and old-fashioned NIMBYism—politicians changed their view as well.

Why has Trump missed the shift? Presumably one reason is that he is surrounded by advisers and tech executives such as David Sacks and Larry Ellison, who are major boosters of and players in the industry. Tech companies invested heavily in Trump at the start of his second administration, lavishing him with gifts, including a gold-plated bauble and donations to projects such as his inauguration and his ballroom, and Trump has reciprocated by taking policy stances that benefit them. Trump may also be personally profiting from the AI boom; his financial disclosures show he’s become more of a tech investor.

Trump has always tended to adopt the latest thing he’s heard, no matter what it is. He has been willing to alienate corporate interests in the past—when he saw some political upside. But he is not hearing from voters who might alert him to how unpopular data centers are. Trump’s rallies and speeches once created a feedback loop in which he conveyed his message to voters and—crucially—they conveyed their thoughts to him. Now, as his energy sinks, his travel schedule gets lighter, and security makes events more challenging, Trump is getting out less.

Though his stump speeches dragged on for hours, Trump was carefully attuned to audience attention and what did and didn’t work. “You know, if it gets a little boring, if I see people starting to sort of, maybe thinking about leaving, I can sort of tell the audience, I just say, ‘We will build the wall!’ and they go nuts,” he told The New York Times in 2016. I think often about a speech Trump delivered in July 2022. It was billed as the launch of a new policy agenda, but as he read it, both Trump and his audience seemed bored. Then he ad-libbed a riff about trans athletes and the crowd came alive. Trump picked up on the shift and emphasized it; trans issues would become a central talking point for his 2024 campaign.

The president has always been susceptible to fake news and bad at filtering information, but rallies provided a gut check about his base, if not about the broader national reality. Now Trump isn’t even receiving that kind of information. One of his major conduits for information is Natalie Harp, a sycophantic aide who isn’t interested in exposing Trump to criticism. He could read public-opinion data, but as his own approval sinks, he has taken to saying (and may well believe) that polls are fake.

As his world shrinks, Trump’s populist touch has faded. Despite being elected twice on an antiwar platform, he’s launched attacks on Venezuela and Iran. As the Iran war has gotten bogged down, he’s been incapable of reading the public mood. He has dismissed voter frustration over rising fuel costs, saying “I don’t even think about” gas; he previously called affordability a “hoax.” In response to reports that American sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln were struggling with a long deployment, Trump said they hadn’t been deployed “nearly long enough.” And the collapse of trade talks with Canada on Friday threatens Republican prospects in border states including Michigan and Ohio.

Each of these cases represents a growing gap between Trump and his base, but none is as ironic as Trump’s stance on data centers. The AI facilities store terabytes of data, but the president can’t get access to the information about them that he needs.

The Trump Comedians Are Tired

By Will Gottsegen

In 2017, as Donald Trump was getting used to the White House furniture, Alec Baldwin was feeling exultant. His impersonation of the new president on Saturday Night Live had made him momentarily inescapable and given the comedy show its highest ratings in years. To capitalize on the momentum, Baldwin co-authored a book-length satirical memoir written from Trump’s perspective. Baldwin’s autobiography—which also came out that year and was excerpted as a cover story for Vanity Fair—noted that his take on the president “seemed to delight nearly everyone in the People’s Republic of Manhattan.” When he accepted an Emmy for his performance in the fall, he addressed Trump directly: “At long last, Mr. President, here is your Emmy.”

It was disorienting, then, to hear Baldwin declare, when I spoke with him earlier this summer, that this sort of comedy has become stale, boring, and useless. “None of it’s funny. I don’t find it funny anymore,” he told me. “There’s nothing left to say about Trump.”

entries.title: Logging In Was Never Supposed to Be This Complicated
entries.summary: Please not another two-factor authentication code.
entries.content:
Please not another two-factor authentication code.

One afternoon earlier this month, I pulled up to the rec center and realized that I had a problem. It was not the three boisterous tweens in the back seat who were clamoring to be set loose in the basketball gym. It was my parking app. I had somehow gotten logged out of Passport Parking, which has become the only way to pay for a spot in much of my town, and it was demanding a four-digit PIN to let me back in. My first guess drew a warning message in red letters: “Invalid PIN. PIN cannot contain 4 sequential numbers, 2 repeated digits, or the last 4 digits of your phone number.” I searched my trusty password manager, which was supposed to spare me these predicaments, but it came up empty. By that point, the kids had run ahead and piled themselves against the gym door, waiting for me to let them in.

Lately, the process of accessing apps and websites has grown dizzying. “I’m in password hell,” a colleague confided to me recently. “Every login attempt is playing the lottery.” The problem is not just the sheer number of digital accounts, all of which require their own password, ideally unique and unguessable (which usually also means un-memorizable). It’s the pileup of solutions to that problem: all of the different layers of software offering to remember your passwords, the six-digit codes sent to your phone, the authenticator apps, the passkeys.

Browsers and operating systems compete with third-party password managers to generate, store, and autofill your credentials. Most of my logins live in 1Password, but others are stored in Apple’s Passwords app (usually by accident), and still others were created via “single sign-on” features such as those offered by Google and Facebook. I vaguely recall certain apps—Facebook is one—prompting me many years ago to copy down a set of “login recovery codes” that would become extremely important should I ever get locked out of my account. Whatever device I stored them on was probably wiped and sold long ago.

Logins have always been a hassle. In the 1990s, forgetting your password sometimes meant mailing a postcard to your service provider and waiting a week or two for it to mail you a new password. In the early 2010s, hackers learned to steal massive troves of logins and then reuse them on other services to steal people’s identities. Things spiraled from there; services started requiring unique, complex passwords with arbitrary requirements. These days, the user experience of logging in is “probably worse than ever,” Troy Hunt, a cybersecurity expert who runs the website Have I Been Pwned, told me. “There’s just no consistency.”

Password managers promised a way out, but they often don’t work as seamlessly as you might hope. I click to autofill my password somewhere, and a 1Password authorization appears, only for an iCloud Keychain authorization to pop up directly over it, preventing me from clicking on the 1Password one. When I manually enter a login I thought I remembered, my browser prompts me to remember it; only after I hit “Save” (pro tip: Do not do this) does the website inform me that the password was not recognized. Even when you log in successfully, there’s the tedious dance of waiting for a six-digit authorization code to appear on your phone or in your email, which defeats the concept of a single password for everything. And if you’re somewhere without cell service or you’re sharing a login with someone who isn’t around, you might just be out of luck.

All of these steps serve a purpose. At least in theory, each added layer helps prevent hacks and breaches. Erring on the side of safety is worth an amount of inconvenience. At the same time, extra steps can introduce security problems of their own. Last year, Hunt fell for a clever phishing scheme when he clicked a link to log in to his newsletter service. His password manager failed to autofill his information, which should have alerted him that something was wrong, he said. But like the rest of us, he was so used to things not working that he went ahead and manually entered his credentials on a site that turned out to be an impostor, designed to steal and exploit them.

None of these obstacles is insurmountable on its own. My problem with Apple’s native password manager fighting with 1Password, for instance, was eventually solved with a 10-minute foray into the bowels of my device settings. But together, they amount to a near-daily irritant. For the less tech-savvy, the situation can be overwhelming. My recent attempts to help my mother fix her password-storage system—which involved loose-leaf notepad sheets full of hand-scrawled credentials scattered around her house like Easter eggs—consumed the better part of a day. By the end, she had all of her credentials updated, validated, and stored in a password manager, just as the experts have been advising for years. But even then, her preferred browser, Google Chrome, showed no interest in surfacing the credentials we had stashed in Apple’s Keychain. And some websites short-circuited her attempts to log in by prompting her to set up a “passkey,” which she interpreted as meaning that her password had failed and she needed to scrap it and set up a new one.

Cybersecurity experts will tell you that passkeys—which typically entail logging in to apps or websites with a face or fingerprint scan instead of a password—are the future. When they work properly, they’re both painless and secure. “It may get to a point where we’re all using passkeys and we don’t even know we’re using passkeys,” Lorrie Cranor, a computer-science professor at Carnegie Mellon University who researches privacy and cybersecurity, told me. “I just say ‘Log in’ and I smile at it, and it gets my passkey, and I’m logged in.”

But that future isn’t here yet, and in the present, passkeys have added a new layer of frustration. Part of the problem is that virtually no one seems to know what they are. “The fact that even I have trouble explaining them should be a clue,” Cranor said. Her past research on the rollout of two-factor authentication suggests that most people tend to resist new security features for as long as they can. Companies can nudge them, but for websites and apps trying to attract and retain users, pushing people to adopt an unfamiliar authentication technology risks scaring them away.

To further complicate matters, passkeys generally aren’t yet replacing passwords altogether, even on sites that use them. Because many passkeys live on your device, one that works on your phone might not work on your laptop, and one that works on your personal laptop might not work on your office device. So you still need a password that works across devices as a backup. It’s a lot, Dave Lewis, 1Password’s global-security adviser, acknowledged to me in an email. “The problem is cognitive overload,” he said. “All these tools are trying to help, but they don’t always work together intuitively.” Still, he disagreed that the situation has never been worse: “When the alternative was using the same password across dozens of accounts or putting it on a sticky note, the fact that people now have password managers, passkeys, biometrics, and multifactor authentication is a good thing.”

The mess might compound before it improves. Hacking attempts have been multiplying as crooks harness AI tools. Companies are adding even more security layers that make logging in harder, and they are pleading for people to make the switch to passkeys. On the bright side, maybe the seamless biometric future is actually within sight, and all of our login woes will soon be over. Then again, that’s what we were promised with password managers too.
